title: Old newspapers sometimes printed ‘etaoin shrdlu’, roughly English’s 12 commonest letters

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still from 1919: an operator’s hands on the many keys of a Linotype keyboard, with a sheet of copy propped above it.
cover.credit: The Ford Motor Corporation · Public domain

body: On a Linotype typesetting machine the keys were arranged by how often letters are used, so the first two columns on the left read **e-t-a-o-i-n** and **s-h-r-d-l-u**. Each key dropped a brass letter mould into a line that the machine then cast in metal, and fixing a slip by hand in a half-built line was slow. Operators instead ran a finger down those first columns to fill out the bad line and threw the result away. Now and then one was overlooked and made it into print, most often in newspapers.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film from 1919: a room of Linotype machines with an operator at work, a close-up of hands typing on a Linotype keyboard, then hands working the machine’s mechanism.

slides.clue: The hot-metal typesetting machine whose letter-frequency keyboard put ‘etaoin shrdlu’ into print
slides.detail: Its keyboard had the sequence etaoin, shrdlu, cmfwyp, vbgkqj, xz twice: once in black keys for lower case and once in white keys for capitals.

slides.question: Why did operators type ‘etaoin shrdlu’ instead of fixing the line?
options: Fixing it by hand was slow
Editors used it to mark ends
It kept the keys from jamming
slides.explanation: Rearranging the letter moulds in a half-built line by hand took too long, so it was quicker to fill out the bad line and discard the cast line of text.
